subtype: Vocal imitation as humour or mockery [Mismatch]
passage: On the school bus in Mumbai, Pranav began copying the driver's habit of saying, “Sit, sit, sit down now,” in a deep, comic voice. Vidya, next to him, giggled. Then Pranav did the same to the conductor, who was walking down the aisle, and the conductor turned around slowly. Pranav stopped. Vidya stopped smiling, too. The conductor said nothing. He just looked, then smiled a little and shook his head. Vidya whispered, “That was a bit much.” Pranav's ears were hot. “I was only playing,” he said. “Maybe check if he's laughing first,” said Vidya.

qa.q: Whose voice did Pranav copy first?
qa.a: The driver's.

qa.q: Why did Pranav say he was only playing, and what else might his hot ears suggest?
qa.a: He meant it as fun, but hot ears suggest he also felt embarrassed once the conductor turned around.

qa.q: What could Pranav try next time he wants to imitate someone?
qa.a: He could look to see whether the other person is laughing too, as Vidya suggested, before continuing.

qa.q: How might the conductor have felt about being imitated?
qa.a: He might have felt mocked or he might have taken it lightly, and his slow turn and small smile leave it unclear.

grounding: A child's imitation of a voice can be play or mockery, and the target's reaction decides.

subtype: Vocal imitation as humour or mockery [Mismatch]
passage: “Hello, class, sit down,” boomed Indu in her deepest voice, hands on hips, and Payal fell off the sofa laughing. “Again! Do Mrs. Nair!” Indu did, with a wobble on the r's. Payal was crying with laughter. “Do Mummy now!” “No,” said Indu, and stopped. “Why not?” “Mummy said the last time I did her, she felt I was making fun.” Payal frowned. “But I like it.” “You laugh, but Mummy didn't.” Payal thought. “Then let's do only the ones who laugh with us,” she said. Indu nodded and did the cook, who chuckled from the kitchen.

qa.q: Whose voice did Indu imitate that made Payal laugh so hard?
qa.a: Mrs. Nair's.

qa.q: Why did Indu refuse to imitate Mummy?
qa.a: She remembered that Mummy felt she was being mocked the last time, so Indu did not want to hurt her.

qa.q: What rule did the girls come up with, and why is it useful?
qa.a: They chose to imitate only people who laugh along, which shows whether it is kind play or unkind mimicry.

qa.q: How might Mummy have felt about the imitation?
qa.a: She probably felt hurt or teased, since she did not laugh, even though Payal thought it was funny. 🙂

grounding: Imitating a voice can be affectionate play or unkind mockery, and the target's reaction decides.

subtype: Vocal imitation as humour or mockery [Mismatch]
passage: I'm Shalini. Keerthana has the squeakiest laugh in our class, like a toy duck. The first time I copied it, just the two of us on the swings, she laughed so hard she fell off, and we did duck laughs all the way home. So last month, in front of the whole class, I did it again when she answered a question. Everyone laughed. Keerthana didn't. She looked at her desk, and her ears went red. I'd been so busy with my joke that I hadn't looked at her. At break I said sorry. Now I only do the duck laugh when she starts it first.

qa.q: What does Shalini say Keerthana's laugh sounds like?
qa.a: Shalini says it sounds like a toy duck.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling when the class laughed?
qa.a: Keerthana felt embarrassed and hurt, as her red ears and eyes on her desk showed.

qa.q: What rule did Shalini make, and why is it a good one?
qa.a: Shalini only does the duck laugh when Keerthana starts it, so the imitation stays shared fun rather than mockery.

qa.q: Why did the same imitation feel different on the swings?
qa.a: On the swings it was just the two friends and Keerthana was laughing too, so it felt like play, not being made fun of.

grounding: Shows the same vocal imitation being affectionate play in private and unkind mimicry in public, with the target's reaction deciding.

subtype: Vocal imitation as humour or mockery [Mismatch]
passage: Class note, Friday. Binita, Class 5. At today's end-of-term party, Gurleen did an impression of me: hands on hips, high voice, “Settle DOWN, children, I can hear a PIN drop!” The class roared, and so did I. She looked at me first, checking, and when I laughed she did it again. That's affectionate play. Ten minutes later, another child copied the new boy's accent, and a few joined in. The new boy wasn't laughing. He was pulling at his sleeve. I stopped the game and said, “Copying is only funny if the person is laughing too. Look at faces first.” Gurleen nodded hardest. Before home time I sat with the new boy, and he's helping me with the notice board next week.

qa.q: What did Gurleen's impression of Binita say?
qa.a: She said, “Settle DOWN, children, I can hear a PIN drop!”

qa.q: What was the new boy likely feeling when others copied his accent?
qa.a: He was likely hurt and embarrassed, since he wasn't laughing and kept pulling at his sleeve.

qa.q: What rule did Binita give the class?
qa.a: Binita said copying is only funny if the person is laughing too, so look at faces first.

qa.q: How did Gurleen check that her impression was welcome?
qa.a: Gurleen looked at Binita first and only repeated it when Binita laughed.

grounding: Shows a child's affectionate imitation of a teacher next to unkind mimicry of a new pupil, and checking whether the target is laughing too.

subtype: Vocal imitation as humour or mockery [Mismatch]
passage: Saturday. Arohi's diary. At lunch I did my Vasudha Dadi impression: “Aye-aye-aye, so much salt, who made this?” Dadi laughed till she cried and said I got the eyebrows perfect. So I tried another one. My brother's voice keeps cracking, going high and low, so I copied it: “Pass the dal, pleeeease.” Nobody laughed. He put his spoon down and went to his room. Dadi said quietly, “With me, you knew I'd laugh. With him, you didn't look.” My face went hot. I knocked on his door and said sorry. He said, “Just don't do it in front of my friends.” Fair.

qa.q: What did Dadi say Arohi got perfect?
qa.a: Dadi said Arohi got the eyebrows perfect.

qa.q: What was Arohi's brother feeling when he put down his spoon?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and hurt at having his cracking voice mocked in front of the family.

qa.q: What did Arohi do to repair things?
qa.a: Arohi knocked on his door and said sorry, and accepted his request not to do it in front of his friends.

qa.q: What was the difference between the two impressions for Dadi?
qa.a: Dadi enjoyed her own impression and laughed, but saw that the brother wasn't laughing, so that one was unkind.

grounding: Shows vocal imitation being loving fun with one person and hurtful mimicry with another, depending on the target's reaction.

subtype: Vocal imitation as humour or mockery [Mismatch]
passage:
Under the peepal tree after school, Raghav did his famous impression of Bholanath the postman: "Chiiiittthi aaayi!" with the bicycle-bell wobble. The postman himself was passing and laughed so hard he nearly fell off his cycle. Everyone cheered.

Encouraged, Raghav turned to Rafiq, who had stumbled over a word in class that morning. "M-m-m-mango," Raghav said, eyes wide. A few boys giggled. Rafiq didn't. He picked up his slate and walked off toward the fields.

Raghav's grin faded. His grandmother, shelling peas on the charpai nearby, called him over. "With Bholanath, who was laughing?"
"Him."
"And with Rafiq?"
Raghav looked at the path. "Only us."

qa.q: What did Raghav's impression of the postman say?
qa.a: "Chiiiittthi aaayi!", with the bicycle-bell wobble.

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling when he picked up his slate and walked off?
qa.a: Hurt and humiliated at having his stumble copied in front of others; he didn't laugh at all.

qa.q: What test did Raghav's grandmother help him use?
qa.a: Check whether the person being imitated is laughing too: Bholanath was, but Rafiq wasn't.

qa.q: How did Bholanath feel about being imitated?
qa.a: He found it funny and laughed so hard he nearly fell off his cycle, so for him it was affectionate play.

grounding: It shows a child's voice imitation being affectionate play with one person and unkind mimicry with another, judged by whether the target laughs too.
